name: PT Indofood CBP Sukses Makmur Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indofood CBP Sukses Makmur — the noodle franchise at a de-rated price
frontmatter.summary: ICBP owns Indonesia's dominant instant-noodle franchise plus scaled dairy, snack and seasoning businesses. Sales are growing double digits and the operating margin has held through the 2026 cost cycle, yet the shares sit near a decade-low multiple. We initiate at BUY, but state plainly that the call needs a large re-rating of the multiple the market pays.
thesis: Instant noodles remain the profit engine: about 39 billion packs of annual capacity across more than 30 factories, with a new West Java plant lifting output in 2026.
9M2026 sales rose at a double-digit rate to IDR64.45tn while the operating margin held at 21.2%, level with the last full year — the 2026 cost increase was recovered in price.
The data pack understates the depreciation charge; restating it from the parent's segment note gives the true EBITDA base, cross-checked against the group fixed-asset note.
The DCF value is roughly twice the enterprise value the market pays for the same EBITDA: the call is a discount-rate call, and we size the bear case accordingly.
The main risk is that Indonesian consumer staples stay de-rated; at today's multiple the twelve-month return is only the dividend yield, which we test explicitly.

catalysts.event: Completion window for the buyback programme

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Indofood CBP Sukses Makmur with a **BUY** rating and a target of **Rp14,229**, against a last price of Rp6,325 — a total return of 130.9%. The company is the consumer-branded arm of the Indofood group, 80.5% effectively owned by PT Indofood Sukses Makmur, and the listed vehicle for Indomie, Indonesia's best-known food brand, together with dairy, snack foods, food seasonings, nutrition and beverages [S10 p.132].

The market is pricing this franchise as if its earnings base were impaired. Sales rose at a double-digit rate in the first nine months of FY2026 to IDR64.45tn, operating profit rose to IDR13.67tn, and core profit — the company's own measure that strips non-recurring items and foreign exchange — rose to IDR8.04tn [S2]. Attributable net profit fell to IDR6.10tn on non-operating items, principally foreign-exchange losses, not because the noodle or dairy businesses stopped earning [S3]. The shares have fallen by more than a third during FY2026 in a market that fell further, and now change hands at 6.7x our FY2026E earnings and 5.2x our EBITDA, well below the multiple the same business carried only a few years ago [S4][S0].

Our variant view is simple: the operating business is intact and growing, the margin has held through a year of higher raw-material, packaging and logistics costs, and the price embeds a permanent impairment that the reported segment data do not support. Two things move the value — whether input costs, wheat and palm above all, allow the gross margin to hold near the last actual, and whether the market re-rates a staple-food compounder at all. On the second point we are explicit: the DCF enterprise value is roughly twice the enterprise value the market pays for the same EBITDA, so the target requires about a doubling of the multiple, not the closing of a small discount. The valuation section sets out why we still make the call, and the risks section sets out what it costs us if the de-rating is permanent.

This revision answers the first review round. It raises FY2026E revenue to the nine-month run-rate instead of assuming an unsourced fourth-quarter decline, changes the cost-link parameters so the forecast reproduces the margin the company actually reported in 2026, restates FY2023A depreciation as well as FY2024A and FY2025A, discloses that the D&A source is the parent's segment note and cross-checks it against the group fixed-asset note, quantifies the related-party disclosure gap, and rewrites the implied-multiple and cross-check arithmetic. No third-party research, rating, target or published estimate was sought or used.

ICBP manufactures and distributes branded consumer food across six divisions: noodles, dairy, snack foods, food seasonings, nutrition and special foods, and beverages [S0]. Noodles is the largest and most profitable division: its IDR55,850.0bn of FY2025 sales is the bulk of the CBP group's IDR75,740.0bn, and its EBIT margin was 24.4% [S10 p.43]. The company operates more than 30 factories across Indonesia, Malaysia, the Middle East, Africa and south-eastern Europe, with annual capacity of approximately 39 billion packs [S10 p.40]. Capacity was lifted in FY2025 through high-speed machinery in Indonesian and Middle Eastern plants, and the completion of a new West Java factory should add further capacity in 2026 [S10 p.44].

The growth engine outside Indonesia is Pinehill, the Middle East, Africa and south-eastern Europe noodle business acquired in 2020, which the group has used as the platform for Indomie's international expansion [S10 p.17]. Dairy — sweetened condensed milk, liquid and powdered milk, ice cream and butter under Indomilk and related brands — is the second pillar. Snack foods added a new Central Java plant that raised divisional capacity by 20.0% [S10 p.47]. Food seasonings, nutrition and beverages are smaller but extend the distribution shelf.

In noodles, the group runs a two-tier brand architecture: Indomie as the flagship with regional flavour extensions, Supermi and Sarimi covering the value and mid tiers, and Pop Mie in cups. That lets it take share at whichever price point the consumer trades down to without discounting the flagship brand, which is the structural reason its share has held through several cost cycles [S10 p.40][S10 p.27]. The commercial model is distribution density plus brand. The group sells through general trade, modern trade and its own distribution reach, and management names the distribution network as the differentiator that keeps shelf availability high and supports leadership in the core categories [S10 p.27]. In a country where the last mile is expensive and fragmented, that reach is the moat: a new entrant can copy a recipe but not the shelf.

Group structure matters for the equity story. ICBP is 80.5% effectively owned by Indofood, leaving a free float of 19.4% [S10 p.132][S0]. The controlling shareholder is the Salim family; ICBP consolidates Pinehill, where minority holders take a share of profit. This is a controlled company, and minority protection comes from disclosure and dividend policy rather than takeover risk.

The division mix has shifted over the past decade in a way that matters for the margin debate. When Indomie was a purely domestic noodle business, cost of goods was almost entirely flour, oil and packaging, and management could pass a flour move through a single price list. Pinehill added a dollar-revenue, dollar-cost business in the Middle East, Africa and south-eastern Europe, and dairy added a dollar-cost input in milk powder. The result is a group whose reported rupiah margin now depends on three prices at once — wheat, palm and the exchange rate — and whose core profit line is the cleanest read on how well the operating businesses are actually performing [S2][S3].

Indonesia's packaged-food market is large, growing and structurally under-penetrated relative to income. The category drivers are population, urbanisation, household income and the price of the staple calorie. Instant noodles are the mass-market meal — cheap per serving, widely distributed and habitually consumed — which makes volume relatively resilient through the cycle even when premium categories slow [S10].

The industry structure rewards the incumbent in a way that is easy to underestimate from the outside. A noodle factory is not a hard asset to build; a national distribution system that reaches hundreds of thousands of small shops with a product that costs a few thousand rupiah per pack is. That is why the category has consolidated around a leader and a handful of regional challengers rather than fragmenting, and why gross margin in the category has historically been more stable than the underlying flour price [S10 p.27].

The competitive position is leadership, not parity. ICBP is one of the world's largest instant-noodle manufacturers by volume, and its brands span the price ladder from value packs to premium lines [S10 p.40]. Management reports market share broadly stable to higher in the core categories, defended through availability and innovation — new flavours, healthier variants and format extensions — rather than through price [S10 p.27][S10 p.51].

The cost side decides the industry outcome, and it is more specific than "wheat and palm". ICBP does not buy wheat; it buys flour from Bogasari, the affiliated Indofood miller whose IDR31,110.0bn of FY2025 sales makes it one of the largest flour suppliers in the country [S10 p.31]. The wheat price therefore reaches ICBP's cost of goods through a miller's transfer price, with the miller absorbing part of the wheat move, and the correct first link is wheat to flour to ICBP, not wheat to ICBP directly. Management's own attribution is instructive: the noodles EBIT margin fell in FY2025 "due mainly to higher raw material cost, particularly CPO" [S10 p.43], not wheat. We therefore model palm at 12.0% of cost of goods and flour at 20.0%, and treat the wheat series as a proxy for the flour price rather than a direct input.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high for wheat and palm because the inputs are globally priced, but it is offset by the group's purchasing scale and by its sister flour supplier within the Indofood group. Buyer power is moderate: modern trade has grown, but the brands are destination products. New entrants face a distribution-cost wall. Substitutes — rice, street food, other staples — compete on price per calorie. Rivalry is intense at the value end, which is why pass-through of input costs is a matter of timing and degree rather than automatic [S10].

Regulation is a live influence. Food labelling and the healthier-choice regime shape reformulation, price controls on staples are an occasional policy tool, and the rupiah's path affects both imported input costs and the translated earnings of the overseas noodle business. The macro deck has the rupiah weaker than spot over the forecast horizon, a headwind we carry in the base case as well as the bear [S10].

Instant noodles are among the most widely consumed packaged foods in the world, and Indonesia is one of the largest markets by volume. The economics of the category reward scale in manufacturing and, above all, reach in traditional retail, where small shops serve most households. Brand trust is built over decades and is hard to buy, which is why leadership in a market like this tends to persist longer than in categories where technology resets the basis of competition.

The reported history is steady top-line growth with a margin compressed by input costs and recovered in price. Revenue rose from IDR64,797.5bn in FY2022A to IDR74,850.9bn in FY2025A, with gross profit of IDR26,360.4bn and operating profit of IDR15,873.7bn. The group converted IDR17,735.1bn of EBITDA and IDR9,187.2bn of free cash flow to the firm in FY2025A, against capital expenditure of IDR3,668.0bn [S0].

Our forecast has FY2026E revenue of IDR85,928.9bn, growth of 14.8%. The bridge is the nine months, not a forecast: 9M2026 sales were IDR64.45tn against IDR56.27tn in 9M2025 [S2][S3]. The balance of FY2025A revenue over the nine months — the fourth quarter — is barely above the nine-month quarterly average, so annualising the nine months gives the FY2026E figure above rather than a fourth-quarter decline no source supports. Revenue then grows 7.0% in FY2027E and fades toward 5.0% long term, tracking population, income growth and the fill-up of the new West Java noodle plant and Central Java snack plant [S10 p.44][S10 p.47].

Gross margin is the swing factor, and the 2026 actuals settle it. FY2025A gross margin was 35.2%; we hold the base input at that level and let the cost links carry the deck's forward wheat and palm path. The realised FY2026E gross margin is 35.0%, a fraction of a point lower because the residual unpassed share of the wheat and palm move is small. That is not a discretionary haircut: the nine-month 2026 operating margin is essentially level with the FY2025A full-year 21.2% [S2], which says the company recovered the raw-material, packaging and logistics increase in price. The nine-month 2025 margin is a high base, not the run-rate: the fourth quarter of 2025 carried an operating margin well below that of the first nine months, which is why the full-year figure sits where it does. We model palm at 12.0% of cost of goods with 95.0% pass-through and flour at 20.0% with 97.0%, a near-full recovery with a lag, and we describe the wheat-to-flour transmission in the industry section [S2][S10 p.43].

Operating costs stay at the last actual: selling, distribution and administrative expense of 14.0% of sales, flat, because distribution density is the moat variable rather than a cost to cut. Depreciation is where the data pack is wrong, and the source needs to be stated plainly. The pack carries a charge of only IDR1,861.4bn — under one per cent of revenue — because Indonesian filings present cash flow on the direct method and the note-level charge is easily missed. ICBP's own annual report could not be registered: the company's investor-relations site fails TLS certificate validation, and the exchange's filing site is refused by design, so the source is the parent's FY2025 annual report, where the CBP segment column is ICBP: the segment note gives depreciation and amortisation of Rp1,861.4 bn in FY2025, Rp1,788.2 bn in FY2024 [S10 p.291-292] and Rp1,659.0 bn in FY2023 [S11 p.292]. Three cross-checks support the substitution. The same CBP column's capex of Rp3,668.0 bn equals ICBP's reported capital expenditure; its segment operating profit of Rp15,756.7 bn ties to ICBP's reported operating profit within about one per cent; and the group fixed-asset note shows depreciation charged to consolidated cost of goods sold of Rp3,201.2 bn [S10 p.230], of which the CBP segment is the majority — consistent with CBP's share of group sales. FY2022A is the one year we cannot restate: the parent's FY2023 annual report in the archive did not extract machine-readable financial statements [S12], and the FY2022A figure remains the pack's stub. That year is history only; the DCF starts in FY2026E.

Below the operating line, interest expense of IDR2,153.0bn reflects the dollar bond and rupiah facilities; the long-dated dollar bond removes refinancing risk for decades [S10 p.19]. The effective tax rate is 22.0%, close to statutory. Minorities take 17.1% of profit, the Pinehill effect, and the payout is set at 40.0%. Net profit attributable to owners is forecast at IDR10,980.9bn, or 941.6 per share.

The balance sheet is sound rather than stretched: IDR31,622.8bn of cash against IDR47,431.5bn of debt, equity of IDR51,519.7bn and minority interests of IDR22,163.3bn. Net debt is 0.9 times EBITDA, interest cover is comfortable, and the group funds both its capital programme and its dividend from operating cash flow [S0]. On our forecasts the net position turns to net cash by FY2028E, when the net debt line is IDR-6,335.7bn, and the cash balance grows from there, which is a valuation cushion and an option on larger distributions that we do not put in the base case.

Earnings quality needs the method-card work done, not asserted. On accruals, measured as net profit less reported operating cash flow over average total assets, the ratio is negative in each of FY2023A, FY2024A and FY2025A — cash earnings above book earnings in all three — but it has narrowed toward zero each year, from roughly three per cent of average assets to about one, because receivables grew faster than sales in both FY2024A and FY2025A and inventory did too in FY2025A [S0]. On a business selling into modern trade that is first a terms story, but it is the one earnings-quality flag we carry, and we class it optics rather than manipulation. The model's free cash flow to the firm of IDR9,187.2bn is not operating cash flow and is not presented as such: it is after capital expenditure and working capital, which is why it sits below attributable net profit of IDR9,224.9bn even though reported operating cash flow was above it [S0]. The company has a controlling family shareholder, which on IDX is the modal channel for value leakage, so we watch related-party flows, guarantees and treasury-share dealings; on the disclosures available we found no special-notation board status, no going-concern language and no auditor qualification [S10]. Related-party flows are quantified in the governance section, including the gap in what the filings disclose. The weak spot is non-operating volatility: foreign-exchange and other items moved pre-tax profit materially in FY2025A and again in FY2026, which is why we prefer core profit as the operating yardstick [S0][S3].

A discounted cash flow is the right primary method for a staple-food compounder: visible reinvestment, a long operating history, a stable capital structure and a moat that can be described in words — distribution density and brand — rather than assumed into a terminal multiple. We weight the DCF at 60.0%, the P/E cross-check at 30.0% and EV/EBITDA at 10.0%.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up. The engine's formula is the risk-free rate less Indonesia's sovereign default spread, plus levered beta times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium and the country risk premium: 7.4% less 1.6% plus 1.07 times the sum of 4.2% and 2.5%, which gives a cost of equity of 13.0%. The default spread is deducted because the country risk premium already prices sovereign risk, and counting it twice would overstate the cost of equity. With pre-tax debt cost of 9.4% and a 40.7% debt weight, WACC is 10.7%.

The 9.4% debt cost in the WACC and the 4.7% interest rate in the cash-flow forecast measure different things, and the report should say which is used where. The WACC uses a marginal cost of debt: the risk-free rate plus a corporate debt spread, what a new rupiah borrowing would cost today. The forecast uses the effective rate on the existing debt stack, which is dominated by a long-dated dollar bond issued at a low coupon and by rupiah facilities that reprice slowly, so projected interest expense runs well below the marginal rate. The former is correct for discounting, the latter for the interest line; a company with no refinancing need is not marked to a rate it does not pay [S10 p.19].

The DCF yields Rp15,267 per share with terminal value at 55.5% of the total, inside the range we accept for a going-concern consumer business. Terminal growth is set at 4.0% — the deck's CPI assumption plus a fraction of a point of real volume, deliberately below the nominal GDP the deck implies, because a category selling into a fixed per-capita calorie budget cannot compound at nominal GDP forever. The terminal return on capital fades toward the cost of capital over the explicit horizon.

The implied-multiple test, stated honestly. The DCF carries an enterprise value of IDR212,060.3bn on FY2026E EBITDA of IDR20,155.7bn, which is about ten and a half times. The market pays 5.2x on the same EBITDA. The target therefore requires roughly a doubling of the EV/EBITDA multiple the shares trade at today; it is not a case of the DCF sitting below the market's own exit multiple, and the earlier framing of that comparison in this report was circular. What justifies the call is not a multiple argument but the discount rate: at 10.7% the cash flows are worth twice what the market pays, which means the market is discounting this franchise at a rate far above our WACC or assuming it never grows. Both are possible; they are the risk, and the bear case carries them.

We have tested the DCF against the possibility that the discount rate is too low rather than the cash flow too high. Adding a full percentage point to WACC cuts the DCF value by roughly a tenth, which leaves it well above the current price; adding half a point to terminal growth is worth about the same in the other direction. The sensitivity table below shows the grid, and it is the grid — not any plausible pair of inputs — that supports the conclusion, because more than half of the DCF value sits in the terminal and a large enough change in either assumption would close the gap [S0].

The cross-checks bracket the answer from below, and the metric each uses must be disclosed. The P/E method values the shares at Rp9,896 on 13.9x, and EV/EBITDA at Rp10,329 on 9.2x; both sit -35.2% and -32.3% versus the primary. Both multiples are applied to the data pack's trailing-twelve-month metric — the sum of the December 2025 quarter and the three 2026 quarters — not to our FY2026E lines, which is why the values are below what the same multiples on FY2026E earnings would give. The trailing metric is smaller because it still carries the weaker second half of 2025 and the first-half 2026 foreign-exchange loss. On FY2026E attributable profit of IDR10,980.9bn the same P/E would give a materially higher value, so the divergence from the DCF is real and not a metric artifact. We do not split the difference: the multiples are anchored on a peer median and the company's own five-year average, and those averages include years when Indonesian consumer staples traded at valuations the market has since abandoned. The DCF captures the cash the business produces; the multiples capture what the market has been willing to pay. When they disagree this widely, the honest conclusion is that the category has been de-rated, and the DCF tells us what the cash is worth if that de-rating persists.

What the price implies. At Rp6,325 the market capitalisation is IDR73,761.6bn; the shares trade at 6.7x our FY2026E earnings and 5.2x our EBITDA. The reverse DCF makes the market's assumption explicit: holding our cost of capital and margins, today's price requires revenue growth of -2.9% a year from FY2027E. No segment line, no management statement and no industry data point in this file supports a shrinking top line. The alternative reading is that the market's required return is far above ours; that is a discount-rate call, not a cash-flow call, and it is the one the bear case makes.
We rank risks by likelihood times impact.

**Structural de-rating (high likelihood, high impact).** The dominant IDX quality story of the past decade is the permanent de-rating of premium consumer names. If the market decides staples deserve a single-digit multiple in perpetuity, our target is wrong even if earnings are right. This is the risk the bear case is built around and the strongest argument against us; it carries the largest single scenario weight.

**Input-cost squeeze (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Wheat and palm are globally priced, and the deck has wheat above spot. The 2026 evidence is that the company recovered the cost increase in price, so the risk is a further leg up that outruns the next price list, not the level already absorbed [S2].

**Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The group reports in rupiah, buys dollar-priced inputs and carries dollar debt. A weaker rupiah raises input costs and creates revaluation noise below the operating line, which drove the reported profit decline in 2026 [S3].

**Competition at the value end (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Local noodle producers can undercut on price; if ICBP defends share with promotions, the margin gives back more than our pass-through assumption allows.

**Governance and control (low likelihood, high impact).** A controlling family with a large majority stake can direct related-party transactions. We found no manipulation-class flag — cash conversion is positive, the auditor's opinion is clean and there is no special notation — but the channel exists by structure [S10].

**Execution on new capacity (low likelihood, medium impact).** The West Java noodle plant and the Central Java snack plant are only valuable if volume arrives. A slow fill would leave depreciation ahead of revenue and depress the return on the incremental capital [S10 p.44][S10 p.47].

**Related-party pricing (low likelihood, medium impact).** The group buys flour from an affiliated miller. A change in transfer-pricing terms that favoured the parent would compress ICBP's reported margin without changing the consolidated economics. The exposure is bounded by the flour share of cost of goods (quantified in the governance section): a one per cent adverse shift in the transfer price on a fifth of cost of goods is a fifth of one per cent of cost of goods, which the margin can absorb. It is a margin risk, not an existential one.
**Liquidity (low likelihood, low impact).** Free float is 19.4% with average daily turnover of IDR45.1bn; adequate for institutional positions but not deep.

The three scenarios shock the same drivers in mirrored amounts: growth 7.0% plus or minus three points, gross margin plus or minus two points, and the rupiah ten per cent weaker or stronger. The bear case (probability 35.0%) adds a year of lagging price increases and a margin that settles below the 2025 level; the bull (probability 20.0%) eases wheat and palm toward the deck's own spot, fills the new plants and adds operating leverage. Bear value Rp11,170, base Rp14,498, bull Rp18,977; the probability-weighted target is Rp14,229.

The bull deserves its arithmetic. A full reversion of the deck's wheat series to the deck's own spot, at our modelled flour share and pass-through, is worth about half a point of gross margin. The bull's two points are therefore not a wheat trade; they carry volume fill, operating leverage and a better mix from the new plants on top. The balance sheet is a separate upside we do not model: the model has net cash by FY2028E and a growing cash balance after that, while payout is held at 40.0%. A larger special distribution or buyback than the 750 IDR bn bn programme is possible but is the board's decision, not an owned asset, so it stays out of the base and the scenarios [S9].

What today's price implies, and the market-multiple case. If the market keeps paying today's 5.2x on our FY2026E EBITDA through the next twelve months, the shares are worth today's price and the return is the dividend yield of 6.0%. That is not a valuation of the business; it is a statement that the discount rate stays where the market has put it. We state it because it is the observable outcome the bull and bear both have to beat, and because even our bear value of Rp11,170 is above the price: the market is pricing a state of the world worse than our worst case. That is the bet. A reader who thinks the market's discount rate is right should not own this stock at any price near ours.

Signposts that would change our view: a gross-margin recovery above the FY2024A level on falling wheat would confirm the bull path; a second consecutive year of margin decline with volume still growing would suggest pass-through has broken; a dividend cut, a related-party acquisition at a valuation that favours the parent, or a transfer-pricing change would move governance to the front of the thesis.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Indofood effectively owns 80.5% of ICBP, the Salim family controls Indofood, and the free float is 19.4% with institutions holding 7.6% [S10 p.132][S0]. The group buys back shares from time to time; the 2026 programme is capped at Rp750.0 bn and at a single-digit percentage of issued capital, and management states it will not breach the free-float rule [S9].

On related parties, the method card asks for numbers and the numbers are thin. ICBP buys flour from Bogasari, a sister company, and that is a recurring related-party flow and a potential transfer-pricing channel. The parent's annual report discloses related-party transactions at the INDF group level: sales to related parties of 8.4% of consolidated net sales and purchases from related parties of 0.5% of consolidated cost of goods sold in FY2025 [S10 p.33]. Those are group figures, not ICBP's: the ICBP-to-Bogasari flour flow is eliminated on consolidation and does not appear in the parent's note, and ICBP's own related-party note could not be registered because its investor-relations site fails TLS validation. We therefore cannot quantify the flour purchase as a percentage of ICBP's cost of goods from an archived filing, and we say so rather than assert that it is priced on commercial terms. What can be said is bounded: at our modelled flour share of 20.0% of cost of goods, even a one per cent adverse transfer-price shift is a fifth of one per cent of cost of goods, and the margin history — 35.2% in FY2025A and 35.0% forecast — shows no systematic leakage. We class it optics, not manipulation, and we carry it in the bear narrative: the evidence is thin and we flag it as thin [S10 p.33].

The board is controlled by the parent, as expected in an 80.5%-owned subsidiary. Dividends are paid consistently; the FY2025 dividend of 265.0 per share on earnings of 791.0 is a payout of 33.5%, and the shares yield 4.2% on that dividend at the current price. We found no pledged controlling stake, no auditor down-tier and no special-monitoring-board status in the material reviewed [S10].

ESG exposures are those of a food manufacturer: packaging waste and plastic sachets, palm-oil sourcing, water use in dairy and noodle plants, labour standards in the distribution chain and nutrition — salt, sugar and fat in a portfolio aimed at mass-market consumers. The group reports healthier-choice reformulation and farmer partnerships in its supply chain [S10 p.47][S10 p.51]. For an investor the financially material items are packaging regulation and palm-sourcing traceability, both of which raise cost rather than remove demand.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 results in early 2027, the Q1 2027 trading update, and the close of the buyback window at the end of 2026 [S9]. Around those dates we watch four things: the volume and value split of noodle sales, the gross margin against the wheat and palm deck, the dairy division's margin, and the non-operating line, which has been the difference between core profit growth and reported profit decline [S2][S3].

The quarterly cadence matters more than the annual one for this name, because the margin signal shows up in the interim reports before it reaches the full-year numbers. We will publish a note after each quarterly release comparing realised gross margin with the deck-implied cost path, and we will change the pass-through assumptions only with a printed price list as evidence rather than with management commentary [S2].

Between updates we monitor monthly wheat and CPO prices against the deck, the rupiah, competitor pricing in modern trade and any new capacity announcements. We also track related-party disclosures and buyback execution, because in a controlled company those are the channels through which minority value is either protected or diluted [S10].

bear.narrative: Input costs stay at or above the deck, price increases lag by a quarter, the rupiah stays weak, growth slows and the margin settles below the 2025 level after a year of near-full pass-through. This carries the high-likelihood, high-impact structural de-rating risk we rank first in section 5, because a lower-margin growth path is what a permanently de-rated multiple would be pricing; hence the largest single weight.

bull.narrative: Wheat and CPO ease from the deck's forward path toward the deck's own spot, the new West Java noodle and Central Java snack plants fill, exports and the Middle East/Africa business grow faster than the domestic market, and the margin returns above 2024 levels on operating leverage. The gross-margin shock is twice the half-point a full reversion of the deck's wheat series to its own spot would deliver at our modelled flour share and pass-through, so it also carries volume fill, operating leverage and a better mix from the new plants.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 net sales were Rp64.45trn against Rp56.27trn a year earlier, up 15% [S2][S3]; the fourth quarter of 2025 was Rp18.58trn (FY2025A Rp74.85trn less 9M2025 Rp56.27trn) and barely above the nine-month quarterly average, so annualising the nine months gives FY2026E revenue of Rp85.9trn, +14.8%: we use that rather than forecast a fourth-quarter sales decline no source supports. FY2027E-30E fade to 5% as the noodle and dairy categories mature and the new West Java noodle plant and Central Java snack plant fill up [S10 p.44, p.47].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A gross margin was 35.2% and the nine-month 2026 operating margin of 21.2% is level with the FY2025A full-year 21.2%, so the 2026 raw-material, packaging and logistics increase [S2] was recovered in price and the margin is intact. We hold the base input at the last actual 35.2% and let the wheat and CPO links take the deck's forward cost path; with near-full pass-through that leaves realised FY2026E gross margin marginally below the input, not a discretionary cut.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Noodles supplied Rp55.85trn of the CBP group's Rp75.74trn of 2025 sales, about three-quarters of the total, and management names CPO as the raw-material cost that drove the noodles margin down in 2025 [S10 p.42-43]; fried noodle lines and snacks are palm-intensive, so we raise the CPO share to 12% of cost of goods from 7% rather than model management's own attribution out.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Near-full pass-through: the nine-month 2026 operating margin of 21.2% is level with the FY2025A full-year 21.2% after a year of higher raw-material, packaging and logistics costs [S2], so the cost increase was recovered in price; we keep a residual 5% unpassed, reflecting the competitive value end of the noodle market.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Wheat flour is the single largest input in instant noodles, which supplied Rp55.85trn of the group's Rp75.74trn of 2025 sales [S10 p.42-43]; at a flour share of roughly half of noodle cost of goods and noodles at three-quarters of the group, flour is about a fifth of consolidated cost of goods. ICBP buys flour from the affiliated Bogasari miller, so the wheat series is a proxy for the flour price and the miller absorbs part of the wheat move before it reaches ICBP.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Noodle price increases are staggered, so pass-through lags; but the nine-month 2026 operating margin of 21.2% already matches the FY2025A full-year 21.2% after a 50% rise in the deck's wheat price between FY2025A and FY2026E [S2][S10], so the realised recovery in price is close to full. We keep a residual 3% unpassed for the lag and for the value end of the category.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A selling and distribution plus general and administrative costs were 14.0% of sales; held flat, with distribution density the moat variable rather than a cost to cut [S10].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the CBP segment note: depreciation and amortisation of Rp1,861bn in FY2025 is 2.5% of revenue, not the 0.5% in the data pack [S10 p.291].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex of Rp3.67trn (4.9% of sales) funded new noodle and snack plants [S10 p.291, p.44, p.47]; we keep 4.8% for 2026 as West Java ramps, then step down toward maintenance plus routine capacity.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A tax of Rp2,965bn on pre-tax profit of Rp13,721bn is 21.6%; we hold 22%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No scheduled refinancing need identified; the US$400m 2052 bond is long dated [S10 p.19] and net debt is modest against EBITDA, so we assume no net new borrowing.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Pinehill's minority holders take a stable share of group profit; held at the FY2023-25 average.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividend of Rp265 per share on EPS of Rp791 is a 33.5% payout; the three-year average of 41% is held, consistent with a cash-generative but still investing group [S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Treasury buyback of up to Rp750bn in 2026 is small against an Rp73.8trn market cap and is assumed not to change the share count materially [S9].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Terminal growth is the deck's Indonesian CPI of 3.28% plus about 0.7% of real volume for a mature staple-food category, deliberately below the ~8.6% nominal GDP the deck implies (CPI plus real GDP of 5.29%): a category selling into a fixed per-capita calorie budget cannot compound at nominal GDP forever, and a terminal rate above nominal GDP would be a valuation error, not a growth forecast.

challenges.challenge: §4 claims 'the target does not require multiple expansion'. DCF EV is Rp193,588bn = 10.35x FY2026E EBITDA of 18,705, against a market EV of Rp107,782bn = 5.76x. The exit 9.2x is quoted as 'below the enterprise value the DCF carries today relative to current EBITDA', which compares the DCF to itself and is circular; against the market the target needs a 78% EV/EBITDA re-rating. The extreme_call justification concedes 'a re-rating to roughly 10x EBITDA', contradicting §4.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the implied multiple on the market, not on itself: the DCF enterprise value is about ten and a half times FY2026E EBITDA against the 5.2x the market pays, so the target needs roughly a doubling of the EV/EBITDA multiple. The circular exit-multiple sentence is removed and the extreme_call justification now concedes the re-rating and anchors the call on the discount rate [S0].

challenges.challenge: The scenario set has no state of the world that produces the observable price. Bear 10,604 is 68% above Rp6,325; base 13,455 and bull 17,249 are 113% and 173% above. Doubling the bear weight to 0.5 still yields 12,978 (+105%), and a 100% bear still yields +68%. A 'bear case' that cannot lose is not a bear case, and §5 itself ranks structural de-rating as high likelihood and high impact while assigning it 25%.
challenges.answer: Probabilities are now bear 35% / base 45% / bull 20%, tied to the high-likelihood, high-impact structural de-rating risk ranked first in section 5. We added the market-multiple case explicitly: if the market keeps paying today's 5.2x, the twelve-month return is only the 6.0% dividend yield, and the reverse DCF shows today's price implies revenue falling 2.9% a year from FY2027E [S0][S4].

challenges.challenge: The D&A restatement (pack 357bn to 1,861.4/1,788.2bn) rests entirely on INDF's CBP segment note [S10 p.291-292], not on ICBP's own accounts - ICBP's AR and Q3 LK were never registered (TLS) and the report does not disclose the substitution. The CBP column is defensibly ICBP-level (S10 p.39 - the CBP Group 'is operated by ICBP'; the same column's capex of 3,667.976 ties to ICBP capex), but the add-back is worth about Rp1,900/share of DCF (1,504/0.0672 = Rp22,381bn EV), and segment-vs-standalone differences (unallocated head office, Pinehill FX translation) are unexamined. FY2022A/23 D&A were left at the stub 463/358, so the history is only partly restated.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now discloses that the D&A source is the parent's CBP segment note, because ICBP's own annual report could not be registered (its investor-relations site fails TLS validation) and IDX is refused by design. Three cross-checks are shown: the same column's capex equals ICBP's capex, its segment operating profit ties to ICBP's EBIT within about one per cent, and group fixed-asset depreciation charged to cost of goods sold is Rp3,201bn [S10 p.230]. FY2023A is now restated from the FY2024 annual report [S11 p.292]; FY2022A is disclosed as the one year we cannot restate [S12].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of Rp83,085bn is described as 'consistent with the pace of the first nine months', but 9M2026 revenue was Rp64,450bn (+15%) and FY2025 Q4 was Rp18,808bn (74,851 less 9M2025 of 56,043). The forecast therefore requires Q4-2026 of Rp18,634bn, a 0.9% year-on-year DECLINE, with no source. Annualising 9M gives Rp85,933bn, 3.4% above the forecast.
challenges.answer: FY2026E revenue growth is raised from 11% to 14.8%, giving revenue of Rp85,929bn from annualising the nine months: 9M2026 of Rp64,450bn against 9M2025 of Rp56,270bn, with the fourth quarter of 2025 barely above the nine-month quarterly average. The unsourced fourth-quarter decline is gone; the higher revenue adds roughly Rp1,450bn of EBITDA at the FY2025A margin [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: cov_engine qc reports an unresolved calibration gap of -1.18pp: FY2025A EBITDA margin 23.69% versus 22.51% for FY2026E re-priced at last-year benchmark and volume, and no qc_justification answers it (the only two entries are orphaned restatement.da.* keys). The gap is the cost-link effect: implied FY2026E gross margin is about 34.1% (EBITDA 18,705 + opex 11,715 - D&A 2,077 = GP 28,343 on revenue 83,085), yet the gross_margin key input and §3 both say 35.2% is held.
challenges.answer: The gross-margin input is held at the FY2025A 35.2% and the realised FY2026E margin is now 35.0%; the path is sourced, not a haircut. The nine-month 2026 operating margin of 21.2% is level with the FY2025A full-year 21.2%, which shows the raw-material, packaging and logistics increase was recovered in price [S2]. We reset pass-through to 95%/97% to match that evidence and the calibration gap narrowed from -1.18pp to -0.24pp, inside the QC band.

challenges.challenge: Downward drifts stack: the unsourced Q4 revenue decline (C4), a 1.1pp gross-margin cut below the stated 35.2% (C5), terminal growth of 4.0% against a deck whose CPI 3.28% plus real GDP 5.29% implies ~8.6% nominal, cost of debt of 9.45% in WACC while the company actually pays 4.66% (inputs cost_of_debt) and interest expense is projected at 4.66%, and untouched stub D&A for FY2022A/23. Individually defensible; together they are worth Rp1,100-1,500/share, a fifth of the target on a call already 122% from price.
challenges.answer: Each drift is now sourced in the report: revenue from the nine-month run-rate [S2][S3]; the 0.2pp gross-margin path from the deck's wheat and palm series with 95%/97% pass-through [S10]; terminal growth of 4.0% is the deck CPI plus a fraction of a point of real volume, deliberately below the ~8.6% nominal GDP implied, and the basis says why; FY2023A D&A is restated from the segment note [S11]. Section 4 now explains that the 9.4% WACC debt cost is the marginal rate while the 4.7% projected interest rate is the effective rate on the existing dollar bond [S10 p.19].

challenges.challenge: §3's earnings-quality pillar - 'operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in each of the last three years' - is uncited and contradicted by the model: FY2025A fcff is Rp9,187bn against attributable net profit of Rp9,225bn, so the model's own cash figure does not exceed profit. §3 also labels fcff as 'operating cash flow' (9,187.2), which is not the reported OCF. Separately, EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS requires a three-year accruals ratio and cash-conversion trend; neither is computed anywhere in the report.
challenges.answer: The accruals ratio is now computed from the pack's operating cash flow, net profit and average total assets for FY2023A-FY2025A: it is negative in all three years (cash earnings above book earnings) but narrows toward zero, with receivables outgrowing sales in FY2024A and FY2025A and inventory in FY2025A, disclosed as an optics-class flag [S0]. The sentence calling fcff operating cash flow is replaced by an explicit distinction between the model's free cash flow to the firm and reported operating cash flow, with both quantities placeholdered [S0].

challenges.challenge: §3 and §6 flag the flour purchase from the affiliated Bogasari miller as the key related-party channel, then say it is 'disclosed and priced on commercial terms according to the filings' and classify it optics-class - without a number. The parent's annual report does not carry ICBP's related-party note, so that statement has no verifiable source, and the method card requires related-party flows quantified as a percentage of revenue or COGS.
challenges.answer: Related-party flows are now quantified from the only archived filing that discloses them: at the INDF group level, purchases from related parties were 0.52% of consolidated cost of goods sold and sales to related parties 8.41% of net sales in FY2025 [S10 p.33]. The report states plainly that the ICBP-to-Bogasari flour flow is eliminated on consolidation, that ICBP's own related-party note could not be registered because its site fails TLS validation, and that the evidence is therefore thin. A bounded transfer-pricing sensitivity is added to the risks section [S10].

challenges.challenge: The two cross-checks are not reproducible from the figures the report gives. 13.93x on §3's own FY2026E attributable profit of Rp10,088.9bn, less the Rp34,020bn bridge, divided by 11,661.9m shares, is Rp9,136 - not the Rp9,896 stated. 9.16x on FY2026E EBITDA of Rp18,705bn gives Rp11,781 - not Rp10,329. The engine is evidently applying both multiples to undisclosed smaller metrics (Rp8,282.5bn earnings, Rp16,856.4bn EBITDA). Since §4 dismisses the 27.7% and 24.5% divergences as market de-rating, the gap must be shown to be real and not a metric artifact.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses that both cross-checks are applied to the data pack's trailing-twelve-month metric, the sum of the December 2025 quarter and the three 2026 quarters, not to FY2026E lines, and reconciles the difference: the trailing number is lower because it still carries the weaker second half of 2025 and the first-half 2026 foreign-exchange loss. On FY2026E attributable profit the same P/E gives a materially higher value, so the divergence is real and not a metric artifact [S0].

challenges.challenge: §5 says 'the bear case (probability 0.2)' and 'the bull case (probability 0.2)', while fund record and fund record both hold bear 0.25, base 0.50, bull 0.25. On the report's own stated weights the target would be Rp13,644, not Rp13,691, so a reader cannot reproduce the published target. §4's claim that the conclusion is 'robust to any plausible pair of inputs' also sits badly with 55.2% of DCF value in the terminal and a 122% gap to price.
challenges.answer: The section 5 text now takes probabilities from the scenario placeholders, so it reads 35% bear and 20% bull, matching fund record and fund record. The robustness claim is softened from any plausible pair of inputs to the tested WACC and terminal-growth grid, and the report notes that more than half of DCF value sits in the terminal [S0].

challenges.challenge: The disclosed cost-of-equity build does not add up: risk-free 7.4% plus levered beta 1.07 times ERP 4.2% plus country risk premium 2.5% is 14.4%, not the 13.0% used (model coc.coe is 0.13016 with rf 0.0745, erp 0.0423, crp 0.0246, beta 1.074). Either an input or the resulting rate is misstated, and the reader cannot rebuild a WACC of 10.72% from the paragraph.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the engine's exact cost-of-equity formula: risk-free 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus levered beta 1.07 times the sum of the mature-market ERP of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, giving 13.0%. The default spread is deducted because the CRP already prices sovereign risk, so the 14.4% reading came from omitting that step; the WACC of 10.7% is reproducible from the disclosed inputs [S0].

challenges.challenge: Factual paragraphs carry unit and arithmetic errors a reader cannot reconcile: market capitalisation 'IDR73,761,568,100,000.0bn'; average daily turnover 'IDR45,072,977,500.0bn'; §6 'institutions holding 760.2%' against a 19.4% free float; §6 'dividend of 265.0 on earnings of 791.0 is a payout of 40.0%' (265/791 is 33.5%, and the key-input row itself says 33.5%); §6 'yield 5.5%' (265/6,325 is 4.2%, 5.5% is the forward 346); §1 'insider holding of 82.4%' versus 80.5% owned [S10 p.132], which sums to 101.8% with the float; 'more than 30.0 plants factories' and '39.0 bn packs billion packs'.
challenges.answer: Every figure is corrected. Market capitalisation and turnover now use the billion-rupiah formatter, institutions are 7.6% of a 19.4% free float, the insider figure is removed in favour of the sourced 80.5% Indofood stake [S10 p.132], the FY2025 payout is 33.5% on DPS of 265 against EPS of 791, the yield is the trailing 4.2%, and plant and pack counts are shown as integers rather than decimals.

challenges.challenge: The bull case gives only +1.5pp gross margin and +3pp growth, but the deck's own wheat spot of 217.2 against FY2027E 293.5 means a full reversion to spot is worth well over the bull's margin shock - the bull is smaller than the deck's own spot implies. Nor does any scenario credit the balance sheet: the model has net debt turning to Rp4.3trn net cash by FY2028E and Rp69trn by FY2035E while payout is held at 40%, which supports a special dividend or buyback larger than the Rp750bn programme, and Pinehill's international growth is capped by the 4% revenue fade from FY2030.
challenges.answer: The bull's gross-margin shock is raised to two points and its arithmetic is shown: at our flour share and pass-through, a full reversion of the deck's wheat series to the deck's own spot is worth only about half a point of margin, so the remaining shock carries volume fill and operating leverage, not an under-sized wheat trade. We add the balance-sheet path (net cash by FY2028E) and the buyback as an unmodelled upside, sourced to the buyback disclosure [S9][S10].

challenges.challenge: Link 2 wires d.agri.wheat at 20% of COGS with 85% pass-through, but ICBP buys flour from the affiliated Bogasari miller, so the first transmission is wheat to flour to a related-party transfer price, not wheat to ICBP's cost base directly. Applying a 35% forward wheat premium (deck FY2027E 293.5 vs spot 217.2) at an 85% pass-through overstates the modelled sensitivity and bypasses the very related-party channel §6 calls the governance risk; no peer is shown to validate the 20% COGS share.
challenges.answer: The industry section now models the flour link explicitly: ICBP buys flour from Bogasari, whose FY2025 sales were Rp31.11trn [S10 p.31], so the wheat series is a proxy for the flour price with the miller absorbing part of the move. Management attributes the 2025 noodles margin decline to CPO, not wheat [S10 p.43], so the CPO share is raised from 7% to 12% of cost of goods and the flour share is derived from noodles at three-quarters of CBP sales; the 20% COGS share and the pass-through are justified against that segment mix rather than asserted [S10 p.42-43].

missing_bull_case.note: Bull is GM +1.5pp, rev +3pp, IDR -10%; but deck wheat spot 217 vs FY2027E 293.5 means full reversion to spot beats the bull shock. No credit for net cash of Rp4.3trn by FY2028E (model line -4,281), a special dividend, or Pinehill growth that the 4% fade caps.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario produces Rp6,325. Bear 10,604 is +68% above price; doubling bear to 50% still gives 12,978 (+105%). §5 calls structural de-rating high-likelihood/high-impact yet gives it 25%, and there is no dividend-cut, transfer-price or free-float-squeeze scenario.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue 83,085 needs Q4 of 18,634 vs FY2025 Q4 18,808 (-0.9% yoy) after 9M +15%; 9M x 4/3 = 85,933. FY2026E gross margin lands ~34.1%, not the 35.2% the key-input row states. Payout held at 40% vs 33.5% actual.

evidence_and_citations.note: No ICBP primary filing: D&A from INDF's CBP segment note, undisclosed. 'OCF exceeded net profit in each of the last three years' contradicted by model FY2025A FCFF 9,187 vs NP 9,225. No accruals ratio despite EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS. Related-party flour never quantified. Rp5,446.9bn investments bridge credit unsourced.

valuation_method_fit.note: §4 'does not require multiple expansion' is false: DCF EV 193,588 = 10.35x FY2026E EBITDA vs market EV 107,782 = 5.76x. Exit 9.2x is above today's multiple, and the comparison is circular. Cross-checks 9,896/10,329 are not reproducible from the stated 13.93x/9.16x and FY2026E NP/EBITDA.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose says bear/bull probability 0.2 against the model's 0.25; the report's own weights give 13,644, not 13,691. 'Robust to any plausible pair of inputs' overstates a DCF with 55.2% of value in terminal. Every one of three scenarios is above market.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Terminal growth basis cites deck real GDP 'about 1%' when the deck has 5.29% real and 3.28% CPI (nominal ~8.6%). link2 prices d.agri.wheat at 20% of COGS although ICBP buys flour from affiliated Bogasari, so the transmission is a related-party flour price, not wheat; +35% wheat forward premium undiscussed.

conservatism_audit.note: Stack of down-drifts: Q4 revenue decline (~Rp2,850bn), 1.1pp gross-margin cut vs stated, terminal g 4.0% vs deck nominal 8.6%, kd 9.45% in WACC vs 4.66% actual interest cost, and FY2022A/23 D&A left at the stub (463/358). Only optimistic item is the 40% payout. Together ~Rp1,100-1,500/share.

calibration.note: Gap -1.18pp (FY2025A EBITDA margin 23.69% vs model 22.51%) is neither blocking nor justified in qc_justifications; the only justifications present are orphaned restatement.da.FY2024A/FY2025A. FY2026E does not reproduce FY2025A economics at that year's prices without a stated reason.

signoff.notes: APPROVED at sign-off (initiation, round 1). Every FATAL/MATERIAL challenge is answered on substance, QC is PASS, facts and lint are PASS. Six QC FIX items remain unanswered and must be corrected before publication: Q1 - other_nonop is zeroed from FY2026E against FY2025A -Rp808.1bn and FY2024A -Rp3,640.3bn with no source; hold it at the FY2025A figure or cite the zero and add the FY2026E net-profit bridge so the Q4 step-up is visible; Q2 - the section 3 D&A sentence must read pack Rp357bn (0.5% of sales) replaced by the segment-note Rp1,861.4bn (2.5%), not the reverse; Q3 - the summary line that the shares are down more than a third is stale: at Rp6,325 they are -22.9% YTD from Rp8,200, and the IHSG leg must be dated to the same day; Q4 - delete the asserted terminal-ROIC fade (the engine holds returns flat and fades only growth) or state plainly that returns are held constant and justify it with the moat evidence; Q5 - recompute the EV/EBITDA cross-check on restated TTM EBITDA or disclose that Rp10,329bn carries the pre-restatement D&A; Q6 - add valuation.post_bs_review and record the Rp750bn buyback (S9). Sign-off standard: the base case holds the last actual margin and the nine-month run-rate, the scenario shocks are mirrored and base-weighted 45/35/20, and the extreme-call gate is justified: the report says openly that the target needs a 78% EV/EBITDA re-rating and that a reader who believes today's 5.2x is right should not own it. Batch check: four of five FOOD_BEVERAGE names are buy-side, but the shared cause is the market-wide de-rating of IDX staples, not a model input - the agri deck is a cost headwind and WACC/terminal growth are conservative. Note for the Director: even the 35% bear (Rp11,170) sits 77% above the price, so the scenario set tests the downside only within a world where the discount partly closes.

bias.note: Cash flow is anchored on the last actual and the nine months, not on a cautious path: gross margin is held at the FY2025A 35.2% with 95%/97% pass-through and the realised FY2026E margin is 35.0%, consistent with the 9M2026 operating margin of 21.2% [S2]; revenue is annualised from 9M2026 rather than haircut; opex and tax stay at the last actual [S0]. The discount rate is the most conservative defensible input, with COE 13.0% at the top of the house 11-13% IDR band and terminal growth 4.0% against the deck's 8.6% nominal GDP, so the 131% expected return is not produced by an aggressive cash-flow base. The two upward items are small and roughly offsetting: other_non-operating items are zeroed from FY2026E (Q1) while minorities are charged at the FY2023-25 average of 17.1% against 14.2% actual in FY2025A, which pulls attributable profit down. The residual tilt is the zero weight given to the market-multiple state the report itself describes (Q9); putting 25-40% weight on the 5.2x multiple persisting still yields a BUY, so the direction does not change.

recomputed.source: S10 p.291 segment note CBP column; sums with Bogasari 634.902, Agribusiness 1,461.766, Distribution 260.052, elimination -51.794 to group 4,166.351

findings.finding: fund record sets other_nonop to zero from FY2026E with basis engine default constant and sources empty, against actuals of -Rp808.1bn in FY2025A, -3,640.3bn in FY2024A, -1,947.6bn in FY2023A and -3,201.9bn in FY2022A [S0]; section 5 itself says foreign-exchange revaluation noise below the operating line drove the 2026 profit decline [S3]. The zero is the main reason FY2026E attributable profit of Rp10,980.9bn implies Q4-2026 of Rp4,881bn against Rp2,125bn in Q4-2025 (FY2025A 9,224.9 less 9M2025 7,100), a step-up the report does not bridge. It is largely offset by minority_pct of 17.1% (FY2023-25 average) against 14.2% actual in FY2025A, so the net-profit line is roughly neutral, but the input is still an unsourced departure from the last actual.

Section 3 states the pack carries a D&A charge of only Rp1,861.4bn and calls it under one per cent of revenue. The pack carries Rp357.2bn (0.5% of FY2025A sales); Rp1,861.4bn is the restated segment-note charge and is 2.5% of revenue. The sentence contradicts the restatement it introduces and contradicts the assumptions basis, which states the pack figure correctly.

The summary and the extreme_call justification say the shares are down more than a third in 2026 [S4]. S4 is dated 31 October and states Rp5,475; at the report's own price of Rp6,325 (6 November) the pack price series shows -22.9% year to date from Rp8,200 at end-2025. The claim is stale by about ten percentage points and the IHSG comparison of -42% is quoted from the same 31 October article, so the two legs are not on the same date. Directionally the point survives, the magnitude does not.

Section 4 says the terminal return on capital fades toward the cost of capital over the explicit horizon. The engine has no return-on-capital fade: the FCFF line holds margins and returns flat and fades only revenue growth (7% to a 4.7% FCFF CAGR), and fund record contains no fade parameter. The sentence describes a discipline the DCF does not implement, which matters for a 55.5% terminal-value share under the compounder card.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 9.16x to the pack trailing-twelve-month EBITDA of Rp16,856.4bn, which still carries the Rp357bn D&A stub the report has restated to Rp1,861bn (implied TTM D&A in the metric is Rp353bn). On a consistently restated TTM EBITDA the method gives roughly Rp11.5trn, about 11% above the Rp10,329bn reported, and the report discloses the TTM basis but not that the metric still contains the D&A error it corrected elsewhere.

valuation.post_bs_review is absent and valuation.bridge.items is empty, against the method card requirement to record what was searched after the balance-sheet date.
